help.settings.system-mode.body: This is the simple option, and the right one for most people. Your volume keys carry on changing the same Windows volume they always did — AorinEQ just draws a nicer pop-up instead of the plain Windows one. If you use Equalizer APO for an equalizer, it is left completely alone. Pick this unless the slider moves but the sound does not change, which is what the other mode is for.
help.settings.eapo-mode.body: Some headphones and USB speakers ignore the Windows volume entirely: you drag the slider, the number changes, and the sound stays exactly as loud. This mode turns the volume down inside Equalizer APO instead, before the sound ever reaches the device, so it always works. The trade-off is that it needs Equalizer APO installed, and the Windows volume slider will sit still while you press the keys — that is normal, not a fault.
help.settings.step.body: How big a jump each press of a volume key makes. 2% is the default and is roughly what Windows itself does. Choose 1% if you like to land on an exact level, or 5% if you would rather get from quiet to loud in fewer presses. You can always hold the key down to move continuously whatever you pick here.
help.settings.device-volume.body: AorinEQ remembers a separate volume for every playback device you use, and switches between them on its own. Unplug your headphones and your speakers come back at the level you last left them, rather than at whatever the headphones were on. There is nothing to set up here — this row just shows you what it has learned so far.
help.settings.tray-left-click.body: What happens when you left-click the AorinEQ icon down by the clock. The default opens a little volume slider, but you can point it at the equalizer or Settings if that is what you reach for most. A right-click always opens the full menu no matter what you choose here, so you can never lock yourself out.
help.settings.tray-middle-click.body: The same idea for the middle button — the click you get by pressing the scroll wheel itself. It is set to mute by default, which makes silencing the PC a single click without opening anything. Set it to do nothing if you press the wheel by accident.
help.settings.tray-scroll.body: Lets you roll the mouse wheel over the tray icon to change the volume, exactly like the Windows speaker icon does. Hold Ctrl while scrolling for fine 1% steps, or Shift for big 10% jumps. It works over a HUD volume widget too, if you have one on screen.
help.settings.scroll-inverted.body: Flips which way the wheel goes. Normally scrolling up makes things louder; turn this on if you would rather scroll down for louder. This is purely personal preference — some people find the inverted direction more natural because it matches dragging a slider downward.
help.settings.autostart.body: Starts AorinEQ quietly when you sign in to Windows, so your volume keys and OSD work from the moment you sit down. It starts minimised to the tray and does not open any window. Leave this off if you would rather launch it yourself when you want it.
help.settings.elevation-state.body: Some games and installers run with administrator rights, and Windows refuses to let a normal program see key presses while one of those is in front. Turning this on makes AorinEQ run with the same rights so the volume keys keep working in those games. The cost is a Windows permission prompt each time it starts, so leave it off unless you have actually noticed the keys going dead in a game.
help.settings.style.body: Chooses what the volume pop-up looks like. The three built-in looks need nothing installed. "Custom skin" uses artwork — your own, or someone else's — and only does anything once you have picked a skin on the Skins page, so set that up first or the pop-up will fall back to the plain look.
help.settings.anchor-top-left.body: Which part of the screen the pop-up appears in. Click any of the nine squares to move it — the grid is a miniature of your screen, so the top-left square puts it in the top-left corner. Bottom-centre is the default because that is where Windows puts its own.
help.settings.offset-x.body: Nudges the pop-up away from the corner or edge you chose, measured in pixels. Useful when something else already lives there — a game overlay, a taskbar on an unusual edge, or a second monitor's bezel. Positive numbers move it right and down; leave both at 0 if nothing is in the way.
help.settings.hide-delay.body: How long the pop-up stays on screen after you stop pressing keys. Shorter gets it out of your way faster; longer gives you time to read the number while you are still adjusting. The timer restarts on every key press, so it never vanishes mid-adjustment.
help.settings.animation-check.body: Fades the pop-up out gently instead of making it disappear the instant the timer runs out. It is purely cosmetic and costs nothing noticeable. Turn it off if you prefer the display to be gone the moment it is done, or if you are recording your screen and the fade is distracting.
help.settings.animation-duration.body: How long the fade takes, once you have turned it on. Shorter feels snappier, longer feels softer. This has no effect at all while "Animate fade-out" is off.
help.settings.hud-edit-switch.body: Widgets are normally click-through, meaning your mouse passes straight through them to whatever is underneath — so they can sit on top of a game without ever getting in the way. Turn this on when you want to actually move them: they become solid, and you can drag them, resize them, and right-click one for its own settings. Remember to turn it back off when you are done, or clicks will keep landing on the widgets.
help.settings.add-spectrum.body: Puts a new always-on-top panel on your main screen showing your own audio. The spectrum shows the frequencies after your EQ, levels shows how close you are to clipping, EQ curve draws your current tuning, and volume shows the level. A new widget lands in the middle of your main screen — turn on "Arrange widgets" above to drag it where you want it.
help.settings.hud-fullscreen-switch.body: Games running in true fullscreen do not share the screen with anything else, so overlays on top of them either flicker badly or simply do not appear. Rather than show you something broken, AorinEQ hides the widgets while such a game is in front and brings them back when you leave it. Turn this off only if your games run borderless-windowed, where overlays work fine.
help.settings.hud-only-playing-switch.bo: Keeps the widgets hidden until sound actually starts, then fades them away a few seconds after it stops. Good if you only want to see them while music or a video is running, rather than staring at flat lines on an idle desktop. Turn it off if you would rather they were always visible.
help.settings.hud-fps.body: How many times a second the widgets redraw. Higher looks smoother; lower uses less of your graphics card, which matters if you are gaming at the same time. One timer drives every widget, so this is the total cost no matter how many you have — 30 is a good balance and 10 is genuinely cheap.
help.settings.skin-credit.body: The artwork the pop-up uses, chosen from the skins you have installed. It only takes effect when the OSD style on the previous page is set to "Custom skin" — otherwise this sits here doing nothing. Skins are just folders of images, so you can make your own or install one somebody shared.
help.settings.skin-designer.body: Everything to do with getting skins onto this PC. The designer builds one from your own images without editing any files by hand; Import installs a skin somebody sent you as a zip; and Folder opens where they all live if you would rather poke around yourself. Nothing here changes which skin is active — that is the row above.
help.settings.protocol-links.body: Lets a web page hand a skin or an EQ preset straight to AorinEQ by clicking a link, instead of you downloading a file and importing it. AorinEQ always shows you what the link contains and asks before installing anything, so a link can never change your setup on its own. Turn it off if you would rather nothing on the web could reach the app at all.
help.settings.open-equalizer.body: Opens the full equalizer: a curve you can drag, presets, AutoEq profiles for headphones, and meters showing whether you are pushing the sound too loud. It has a simple three-slider view as well as the full editor, so it is worth opening even if "parametric equalizer" means nothing to you. Your tuning is saved per playback device.
help.settings.air-play-status.body: Pick a HomePod, Apple TV or other AirPlay speaker on your network and press Connect to start sending this PC's sound to it. They are found automatically — press Refresh if yours is not listed yet, as some devices take a few seconds to answer. Connecting takes about half a second, during which the window will not respond; that is normal.
help.settings.air-play-source.body: Which of this PC's playback devices gets captured and sent. Left on the default, whatever you are already listening to is what gets streamed — which means it plays in both places at once. If you want the sound to come out of the AirPlay speaker only, the dependable way is to install a virtual audio device and choose it here.
help.settings.air-play-mode.body: How much sound is sent ahead of time. Sending more makes dropouts far less likely but adds a delay between what you see and what you hear, which matters for video and games and not at all for music. Start with Normal, and only move to Real-time if the delay bothers you — then watch the resend figure below, because a rising number means the network cannot keep up.
help.settings.air-play-volume.body: The speaker's own volume, the same one its buttons or the Home app would set. The simplest setup is to leave this at 100% and change loudness with your volume keys as usual, exactly as you would with any other speaker. Turning it down here as well just means both controls are fighting over the same thing.
help.settings.air-play-retarget-note.bod: While streaming, your volume keys can either change this PC's volume or the AirPlay speaker's. Which one is correct depends on the mode you chose on the Volume page, so AorinEQ decides for you rather than letting you get it wrong. In Equalizer APO mode the sound is already turned down before it is sent, so changing the speaker as well would quieten it twice — that is why this greys itself out and explains rather than simply disappearing.
help.settings.air-play-mute-local.body: Silences this PC's own speakers so the sound only comes from the AirPlay device. Whether it works depends entirely on your sound hardware: on some machines muting the PC also mutes the stream, leaving you with silence everywhere. It is off by default for that reason, and choosing a virtual device as the Source above is the reliable way to get the same result.
help.settings.air-play-dither.body: Some speakers power down part of themselves when the sound stops, then take a moment to wake up — so the first fraction of a second of the next track gets clipped off. This sends an extremely quiet noise instead of true silence, far too soft to hear but enough to keep the speaker awake. Leave it on unless you have a reason not to; it costs nothing and does not touch the music itself.
help.settings.air-play-idle-seconds.body: Keeps the connection open when nothing is playing, so the next track starts instantly instead of pausing while everything reconnects. The cost is that the speaker stays claimed by this PC, so another device cannot take it over. Turn it off if you share the speaker with a phone or a tablet and want AorinEQ to let go after a while.
help.settings.auto-update.body: Checks for a newer AorinEQ when it starts and once a day after that, and installs it for you. Updates are downloaded from the project's own release page and checked against a published fingerprint before anything is replaced, so a corrupted or tampered download is refused rather than installed. Turn it off if you would rather decide when to update.
help.settings.update-status.body: Checks for a newer version right now, without waiting for the daily check. Useful if you have just been told a fix is out. If an update is found it is downloaded and applied the next time AorinEQ starts, so nothing is interrupted while you are using it.
